power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P=0.14 ", "P=0.136 "), Sentence = c("Imputed and original data distributions were statistically similar; the lowest P value was observed for NRAS status (set #2; 4.8% vs 7.6%; P=0.14 KaroLiver, and set #3 6.3% vs 14.7%; P=0.136 OSLO-COMET; Fig. S2 & S3).", "Imputed and original data distributions were statistically similar; the lowest P value was observed for NRAS status (set #2; 4.8% vs 7.6%; P=0.14 KaroLiver, and set #3 6.3% vs 14.7%; P=0.136 OSLO-COMET; Fig. S2 & S3)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Introduction: Treatment strategies for colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) are increasingly complex, driving interest in advanced prognostic tools.
Externally validated benchmarks based on established clinical risk scores are needed to contextualise emerging models.

However, existing scores remain difficult to apply and compare, because they provide categorical risk strata rather than individualised probabilities, and because model parameters are rarely published.
Here, we validate and recalibrate seven established risk scores to derive individualised recurrence probabilities for future score benchmarking.
Despite curative-intent surgery, recurrence after resection of colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) remains a major clinical challenge, affecting up to 70% of patients 1- 5 .
text.formatted: Despite curative-intent surgery, recurrence after resection of colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) remains a major clinical challenge, affecting up to 70% of patients <ref type="bibr">1- 5</ref> .

text.text: Management of CRLM has become increasingly complex as patient selection, surgical approaches, and systemic therapies have evolved 6 .
text.formatted: Management of CRLM has become increasingly complex as patient selection, surgical approaches, and systemic therapies have evolved <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: Surgical strategies have expanded toward parenchymal-sparing techniques and thermal ablation 7, 8 , while liver transplantation is now considered for selected patients 9, 10 .
text.formatted: Surgical strategies have expanded toward parenchymal-sparing techniques and thermal ablation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> , while liver transplantation is now considered for selected patients <ref type="bibr">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: Concurrently, systemic therapies are becoming increasingly effective 11 .
text.formatted: Concurrently, systemic therapies are becoming increasingly effective <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: Although these advances are currently limited to subgroups of patients, they underscore a general shift in the management of CRLM: while technical resectability remains the central criterion, clinical decisionmaking increasingly requires integrating tumour biology and patient-specific factors into a multidisciplinary framework, ideally informed by individualised estimates of recurrence risk.

Various prognostic scores have been developed to predict recurrence and survival after CRLM resection [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] , and many have undergone external validation in contemporary cohorts [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] .
text.formatted: Various prognostic scores have been developed to predict recurrence and survival after CRLM resection <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> , and many have undergone external validation in contemporary cohorts <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> .

text.text: Nevertheless, these scores are rarely integrated into routine practice due to specific hurdles to their implementation: most existing models express risks as ordinal scores or categorical strata rather than time-specific probabilities, limiting their interpretability.
Moreover, performance evaluation is often restricted to measures of discrimination, without assessment of calibration or performance at clinically meaningful time points 22 .
text.formatted: Moreover, performance evaluation is often restricted to measures of discrimination, without assessment of calibration or performance at clinically meaningful time points <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> .

text.text: Even when models have been externally validated, the underlying regression coefficients and model intercepts are rarely reported, precluding direct recalibration and adaptation to new populations.

Hence, novel prognostic tools based on emerging methods such as circulating tumour DNA 23, 24 or advanced radiological image analyses [25] [26] [27] can only be indirectly compared with existing clinical scores, and efforts to compare and integrate established models with novel approaches have been limited.
text.formatted: Hence, novel prognostic tools based on emerging methods such as circulating tumour DNA <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">24</ref> or advanced radiological image analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[27]</ref> can only be indirectly compared with existing clinical scores, and efforts to compare and integrate established models with novel approaches have been limited.

text.text: Here, we evaluate seven clinical risk scores in a comprehensive framework that included discrimination, calibration, and net benefit analyses at multiple clinically relevant time points.

We translate them into individualised, percentage-based recurrence probabilities, and publish all model parameters and source code through an open-source online calculator to enable future adaptation and benchmarking.

For score validation and model recalibration, this retrospective observational study was based on the KaroLiver cohort, which included consecutive patients 18 years or older who underwent curative-intent liver intervention at the tertiary centre, Karolinska University Hospital, Stockholm, Sweden, from 2013 to 2021 (follow-up to 2025).

Validation was performed in the OSLO-COMET randomised controlled trial 28 , which included patients from 2012 to 2016 (follow-up to 2022) at the tertiary centre, Oslo University Hospital, Oslo, Norway 28 .
text.formatted: Validation was performed in the OSLO-COMET randomised controlled trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">28</ref> , which included patients from 2012 to 2016 (follow-up to 2022) at the tertiary centre, Oslo University Hospital, Oslo, Norway <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">28</ref> .

text.text: KaroLiver was approved by the Swedish National Ethical Review Authority (EPM 2019-01571, amendments 2020-00428, 2021-06863-02, 2022-06588-02, and 2025-05423-02); informed consent was waived.

The study was not preregistered, and the study protocol was not published prior to the study.
Patients or patient advisory bodies were not involved in the study.
KaroLiver included patients with histologically confirmed colorectal carcinoma and radiologically confirmed liver metastases.

Patients were reviewed by a liver-specific multidisciplinary team (MDT); in the event of disease recurrence, MDT re-evaluation was performed, with curative-intent retreatment pursued when technically feasible and oncologically appropriate.
Patients treated with ablation only were not included.
Patients with extrahepatic disease were included when amenable to complete curative-intent treatment.
To meet the assumption of full outcome observation for all subjects in generalised linear models, 28 patients who were lost to follow-up at 3 years were excluded from model recalibration (Fig. S1a).

text.text: Inclusion criteria for OSLO-COMET have been previously described (Fig. S1b) 3, 28 ; it enrolled patients amenable to parenchyma-sparing resection, comparing open with laparoscopic techniques.

text.text: For both cohorts, chemotherapy was administered according to the local guidelines in effect at the time of each patient's treatment, principally aligned with the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Guidelines.
Postoperative surveillance consisted of thoracic and abdominal contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) and tumour marker measurements at the treating physician's discretion.
Baseline recommendations differed: in KaroLiver, every 3 to 6 months; in OSLO-COMET, every 4 months until 2 years after surgery, then every 6 months.
For KaroLiver, data were retrospectively extracted from electronic patient records.
Variables included patient age and sex, primary metastases tumour characteristics.
Mutational and microsatellite instability/mismatch repair testing were performed on a per-demand basis in clinical routine.
Data for OSLO-COMET were collected as previously described 28.
text.formatted: Data for OSLO-COMET were collected as previously described <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">28</ref>.

text.text: In KaroLiver, disease-free interval (DFI) was defined as the time between diagnosis of CRC and CRLM, and synchronous disease as DFI <1 month.
text.formatted: In KaroLiver, disease-free interval (DFI) was defined as the time between diagnosis of CRC and CRLM, and synchronous disease as DFI <1 month.

text.text: In OSLO-COMET, DFI was recorded to indicate whether CRLM was diagnosed within 12 months of CRC diagnosis.

Recurrence-free survival (RFS) was defined as the time from CRLM resection to first confirmed recurrence, including local or distant recurrences documented radiologically, endoscopically, or clinically.
Patients alive and without confirmed recurrence were censored on the date of last imaging in KaroLiver, or last documented follow-up in OSLO-COMET.
Established clinical risk scores were calculated according to the original score definitions.

These included extensively validated and cited scores 20 (Fong, Konopke, Nordlinger, Nagashima) 12, 13, 15, 30 , and recent scores incorporating tumour-biological variables such as histology (Helsinki) 14 and/or genetic variant background (Genetic And Morphological Evaluation [GAME] score, modified clinical score [m-CS]) 31, 32 .

Internal validation of the recalibrated models was performed using bootstrapping in KaroLiver; models were externally validated in OSLO-COMET.

text.text: We followed a stepwise process: using a real-world consecutive cohort, we (1) validated established clinical risk scores, (2) recalibrated them to provide individualised risk percentages, and (3) developed a web-based calculator that (4) was validated in an external cohort (Fig. 1a).

text.text: In KaroLiver, 709 patients (median age 67 years [IQR, 59-74 years]; 434 males [61%]) underwent their index CRLM resection.
A total of 422 patients (60%) had synchronous metastases, and 444 (63%) received neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
Major hepatectomy was performed in 313 patients (44%).
Information on mutational status was available for 314 patients (44%).

Despite differences in patient selection, recurrence timing was broadly comparable between cohorts, while the recurrence rate was lower in OSLO-COMET (median RFS 14.3 [95%CI 11.1-20.0] months vs 10.9 [95%CI 9.2-12.4] months; recurrence rates 6.0% vs 12.3%; P=0.009; Fig. 1b).

text.text: After a median follow-up of 44.9 months (95% CI, 41.1-49.5 months), recurrence occurred in 467 of 709 patients (65.9%), most commonly in the liver (191 of 467 [40.9%]) and lung (98 of 467 [20.9%]).
The median time to recurrence was 7.1 months (95% CI, 6.5-7.6 months).
The 1-year and 3-year RFS rates were 46.5% (95% CI, 42.8%-50.6%) and 28.3% (95% CI, 24.9%-32.1%), respectively.
Median OS was 51 months (95% CI, 46.1-59.6 months, compared with the median RFS of 10.9 months [95%CI 9.2-12.4]).
The 3-year and 5-year OS rates were 61.3% (95% CI, 57.8%-65.1%) and 45.6% (95% CI, 41.8%-49.8%), respectively.
Seven established clinical risk scores predictive of RFS and/or OS were validated (Fig. 1C).

text.text: Time-dependent AUC analyses revealed improved performance at later time points after surgery.

At 6 months, the Nordlinger score nominally showed the highest AUC Among more recent scores, the Helsinki, m-CS, and GAME scores classified 156 (22.0%), 254 (35.8%), and 358 of 709 patients (50.5%) as high risk, with median RFS of 6.0, 7.2, and 7.6 months, respectively.

The highest-risk classes of the Nagashima, Fong, and m-CS scores showed limited discriminative utility using their pre-defined strata, classifying only 4 (0.6%), 5 (0.7%), and 34 of 709 patients (4.8%), respectively.
Intermediate-risk classification was the most consistent across the scores, including 280 (39.5%) to 410 (57.8%) of 709 patients, with median RFS ranging from 10.6 to 15.4 months.
The Nagashima score was an exception, classifying fewer patients (117 of 709 [16.5%]) as intermediate risk with a notably shorter median RFS of 6.0 months.

Despite a known moderate association between RFS and OS after CRLM resection 33 , which was confirmed in KaroLiver (Kendall's t 0.52, 95%CI [0.48-0.57], P<0.001), all scores also significantly stratified OS (log-rank P<0.001; Fig. S4).

text.text: To evaluate score performance with calibration and clinical utility assessments at relevant time points, we recalibrated the scoring models to a probabilistic scale (Fig. 1a, box 2).

text.text: Inspection of calibration plots confirmed successful recalibration: mean observed event rates closely followed a 45-degree line, indicating overall agreement between predicted and observed risks (Fig. S9).

text.text: Most scores demonstrated good agreement between predicted and observed recurrence probabilities, with observed-to-expected ratios close to unity across scores and time points in KaroLiver after internal validation, and in the OSLO-COMET cohort (Fig. 3, Fig. S10, Table S2).

text.text: At 6 months, Fong, Nagashima, and Nordlinger scores overestimated recurrence risk at higher predicted probabilities (>50%) in KaroLiver.

text.text: Although agreement between observed and predicted risks was generally good at 1 to 3 years in both cohorts, categorical risk classifications did not always correspond to predicted or observed probabilities.

For example, the Nagashima score classified patients as low risk despite predicted recurrence probabilities ranging from 25% to 75% at 1 to 3 years, respectively (Fig. 3), favouring a probabilistic approach.

text.text: Two scores incorporated postoperative variables, including resection margin (Nordlinger) and maximum tumour viability, as well as vascular and biliary invasion (Helsinki).

Comparing the performance of these scores with and without postoperative variables (Table S3, Fig. S11) revealed slightly lower performances (mean ΔAUC at 6 months to 3 years +0.02 [95% CI -0.001 to +0.05] for Helsinki and +0.01 [95% CI -0.0006 to -0.02] for Nordlinger).

text.text: In KaroLiver, most recalibrated scores showed higher net benefit than default strategies that would assume uniform high or low risk for all patients (Fig. 4), with the GAME score yielding the highest net benefit across most time points and threshold probabilities.

text.text: The m-CS score provided the least incremental benefit.
Results in the OSLO-COMET validation cohort were concordant.

The regression model coefficients derived from score recalibration (Table S4) were used to develop PLATO (Personalised Liver metastases risk AssessmenT in Oncology; www.plato-calc.org), an open-source calculator for individualised recurrence risk estimation after CRLM resection.

text.text: PLATO accepts input for the variables required by each validated score, and returns individualised recurrence probabilities at 1, 2, and 3 years after resection, along with the corresponding categorical risk classification from each original score.

Its source code, including score calculation, recalibration, and validation pipelines, is publicly available (https://github.com/vilja-a/plato-crlm-risk-prediction/), enabling independent verification, adaptation, and integration of future risk scores.

text.text: This study evaluated seven established CRLM risk scores, made the model parameters openly available, and developed PLATO, an online tool that provides individualised recurrence probabilities.
External validation supported the generalisability of the probabilistic prediction approach.

A central contribution is the conversion of categorical risk strata into percentage-based estimates for all scores, making validated prognostic evidence clinically actionable and enabling direct benchmarking of novel scores.
The published coefficients and source code provide an adaptable reference framework for future score calibration, validation, and comparison.
KaroLiver is comparable to other contemporary cohorts with respect to median age, sex distributions, surgical approaches, and molecular profile [38] [39] [40] [41] .

text.text: Its 5-year OS is consistent with the LiverMetSurvey benchmark 42  To our knowledge, this study provides the first validation of the Helsinki score, which incorporates postoperative histological variables.

text.text: Adding these histological variables to the Helsinki and Nordlinger scores did not meaningfully improve discrimination, suggesting that classical histological parameters provide limited independent information beyond conventional clinical data in this setting.
There is limited correlation between RFS and OS after CRLM resection, likely due to distinct biological and treatment-related determinants of each outcome 33 .
text.formatted: There is limited correlation between RFS and OS after CRLM resection, likely due to distinct biological and treatment-related determinants of each outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">33</ref> .

text.text: Disease trajectories after CRLM resection are heterogeneous and include liver-only, lung-only, and mixed recurrences that might be amenable to curative-intent treatment.
This heterogeneity complicates the use of OS as an endpoint because of increasingly complex and effective postrecurrence treatments.

Against this background, the clinical rationale for using RFS as the prognostic target becomes stronger, since RFS more directly reflects tumour biology rather than the variable downstream treatment course.
Beyond binary recurrence, the concept of "treatable recurrence," amenable to curative-intent retreatment, represents a clinically relevant refinement not yet captured by current scores.
Models targeting early extrahepatic recurrence partly address this 43 , but scoring systems have yet to integrate recurrence patterns into individualised probability estimates 43.
text.formatted: Models targeting early extrahepatic recurrence partly address this <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">43</ref> , but scoring systems have yet to integrate recurrence patterns into individualised probability estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">43</ref>.

text.text: A recent study compared multiple risk scores and, in line with our results, demonstrated that most established scores significantly stratified patients by OS, although discrimination was modest across models 44 .
text.formatted: A recent study compared multiple risk scores and, in line with our results, demonstrated that most established scores significantly stratified patients by OS, although discrimination was modest across models <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">44</ref> .

text.text: The study provided a valuable head-tohead comparison of established scores; however, calibration, net benefit, external validation, and translation into individualised probability estimates were beyond its scope.

Previous calculators have advanced individualised prognostication [45] [46] [47] [48] [49] [50] , but several limitations restrict direct benchmarking and clinical translation: reliance on machine learning models with limited parameter transparency 45, 46 , absent external validation, unavailability of model parameters, restriction to selected patient subgroups 48 , and focus on long-term outcomes 50 .

text.text: We address these limitations by providing individualised probability estimates at clinically relevant time points, grounded in established scores with documented validation histories, and by publishing source code and model coefficients.
Next-generation clinical risk scores will increasingly incorporate molecular tumour profiling, including sequencing, imaging-based machine learning, and other highdimensional data.

As clinical decision support moves toward AI-based systems 51 , validated and interpretable risk scores remain essential: broad clinical trust in AIgenerated recommendations requires transparent, externally validated benchmark models against which their outputs can be contextualised.

text.text: By publishing open model coefficients alongside calibration and decision-curve analyses, we aim to provide a transparent, reproducible reference against which such future prognostic tools can be evaluated, as treatment options and prognostic variables evolve.
While this study builds on the established clinical risk scores, offering extensive evaluation, a transparent workflow and improved accessibility via PLATO, several limitations are worth noting.

First, both cohorts consist predominantly of patients with European ancestry treated within publicly funded health systems, which limits generalisability to populations with differing disease biology, treatment access, or healthcare structures.
Second, genetic variant data were available for 44% of KaroLiver patients, necessitating imputation and potentially affecting the robustness of the m-CS and GAME scores.

Finally, differences in postoperative surveillance intervals between cohorts, every 3 to 6 months for KaroLiver and every 4 months for OSLO-COMET, may have introduced bias in the timing of recurrence detection.
Despite these limitations, our findings provide a transparent foundation for future prognostic score development and benchmarking with openly available model parameters.

Properly recalibrated and externally validated, these established clinical risk scores provide the reference frame against which next-generation prognostic models can be measured -and PLATO makes that comparison clinically accessible.

text.text: In low-risk groups, long median RFS was reached among Nordlinger, GAME and Helsinki scores: using the originally published strata, the Nordlinger score classified 59 of 709 patients (8.3%) as low risk with median RFS of 39.6 months, GAME 155 of 709 patients (21.9%), with median RFS of 82.5 months, and Helsinki 71 of 709 patients (10.0%), with median RFS not reached.
Konopke and Nordlinger scores classified 168 of 709 patients (23.7%) and 240 of 709 patients (33.8%), respectively, as high risk, with a median RFS of 6.1 months for both.

Successful validation in OSLO-COMET, a trial cohort with substantially different inclusion criteria, supports the robustness and generalisability of the probability estimates.All scores significantly stratified RFS, confirming their discriminative value in both cohorts, although performance varied across scores and follow-up intervals.

The clinical value of a score depends on the decision it supports, and the meaningful threshold range differs accordingly; intensified surveillance favours lower risk thresholds at earlier time points, where the cost of missing recurrences outweighs that of unnecessary imaging.
Adjuvant therapy selection warrants higher thresholds at later time points, where treatment burden must be proportionate to recurrence risk.

Hence, probability estimates are most informative when the decision context is defined, and future score/model development would benefit from clinically motivated, a priori defined performance targets, tailored to each scenario.
Decision curve analysis demonstrated that the GAME score had the highest net benefit at 1 and 2 years.

Score performance at lower thresholds and earlier time points remained limited across all scores, highlighting an unmet need that future purpose-built models could address; accordingly, the 6-month time point was not included in PLATO.
